name: Castle Fraser

description:
Castle Fraser stands within its own 300-acre estate near Kemnay in Aberdeenshire, and it ranks among the most architecturally ambitious of the so-called 'Castles of Mar' — a loose grouping of grand tower houses raised across this stretch of Aberdeenshire by families competing, in effect, to build the most impressive fortified residence their wealth could support. Building began in 1455, when Thomas Fraser constructed a fortified house he named 'Castle of Muchil-in-Mar,' a considerably more modest structure than the building that stands today. That original house was transformed in 1575, when Michael Fraser of Stoneywood rebuilt it on a far grander scale as a Z-plan tower house — a distinctive Scottish fortification layout in which two towers project diagonally from opposite corners of a rectangular main block, giving defenders overlapping fields of fire along every wall. Most of the castle visible today was complete by around 1636, the product of more than a century and a half of sustained Fraser family ambition and investment.

Castle Fraser is widely regarded as one of the largest tower houses in Scotland and one of the most elaborate Z-plan examples anywhere in the country, executed in a late Renaissance and early Baroque interpretation of Scots Baronial style: richly carved and ornamented stonework, crow-stepped gables, and boldly corbelled turrets project from the walls in a display of architectural confidence matched by few comparable Scottish houses. The Fraser family occupied the castle continuously for more than four hundred years, and that long single-family tenure has left the building unusually rich in personal material — portraits, objects and mementos throughout the rooms trace the individual stories of successive lairds rather than presenting a generic period interior.

The castle's interior underwent a significant remodelling between 1820 and 1850, commissioned by Charles Fraser from two of the leading Scottish architects of the era working in sequence: William Burn prepared proposals for relatively minor alterations around 1816, before John Smith took on more substantial expansion work between 1830 and 1836. Smith's most celebrated contribution is the Library, designed around 1830, which blends his characteristic Regency sensibility with Tudor-inspired detailing — a genuinely accomplished room that stands as one of the highlights of any visit to the castle's interior, distinct in character from the more overtly defensive character of the building's exterior and older rooms.

The grounds surrounding the castle extend across more than 300 acres of parkland, woodland and farmland, including a 19th-century walled kitchen garden that remains a highlight for garden-focused visitors. Much of this landscape bears the direct imprint of Elyza Fraser, remembered as the estate's 'lady laird,' who oversaw a significant reshaping of the grounds — removing the original formal gardens and orchards in favour of a more naturalistic parkland style then coming into fashion, and commissioning the estate's eye-catching octagonal stable block, a genuinely unusual and memorable piece of estate architecture in its own right. Castle Fraser passed out of family ownership in 1976, when it was gifted to the National Trust for Scotland, which manages the property today.

Castle Fraser also appears as a stop on a real, bookable multi-day tour: Rabbie's Small Group Tours' 'Scottish Highlands 4-Day Castle Tour From Edinburgh' visits the castle's walled garden on its second day, en route to Crathes Castle later the same afternoon, with entry to Castle Fraser included in the tour package — a genuine option for visitors who would rather see Castle Fraser as part of a guided multi-day Highlands itinerary than as a standalone day visit.

how_to_visit:
**Getting there:** Castle Fraser is near Kemnay in Aberdeenshire, roughly 16 miles west of Aberdeen. The castle is best reached by car; there is no direct rail or regular bus service to the site itself.

**Tickets:** Direct entry via the National Trust for Scotland costs £18 for adults, £14 concession, £40.50 for a family, and £34.50 for a one-adult family — verify current prices on the NTS website before visiting, as these are subject to seasonal review. The castle, shop and tea room are open 10:30–16:30 (last entry 15:30); the walled garden 10:00–16:00; the grounds dawn to dusk year-round.

**Guided multi-day option:** Rabbie's Small Group Tours' 'Scottish Highlands 4-Day Castle Tour From Edinburgh' (small groups, maximum 16 people) includes a stop at Castle Fraser's walled garden on Day 2, continuing to Crathes Castle later that day, with entry to Castle Fraser covered by the tour price. This suits visitors building a longer Highlands itinerary rather than a single-castle day trip.

**Stay in the castle itself:** Castle Fraser's East Wing offers a two-bedroom, ground-floor apartment within the historic building — a fully equipped kitchen, washing machine, fireplace and smart TV, with access to the estate's traditional walled garden. It sleeps up to 4 across one king and one twin bed, and sits a short walk from the castle itself, about 14 miles from Aberdeen Airport. This is a separate booking from the day-ticket entry: it suits visitors who want to spend the night literally inside the historic building, rather than an alternative to visiting the castle's staterooms.

**Combine with:** Crathes Castle and Dunnottar Castle, both within reach of Aberdeenshire's dense concentration of historic houses, make natural additions to a Castle Fraser visit for anyone exploring the region beyond a single stop.

faqs.question: Can I stay overnight inside Castle Fraser itself?
faqs.answer: Yes. The castle's East Wing offers a two-bedroom, ground-floor apartment within the historic building, sleeping up to 4 guests, with a fully equipped kitchen, fireplace and access to the estate's walled garden. This is a separate booking from the day-visit ticket — it's an additional option for anyone who wants to spend the night inside the historic building itself, not a substitute for visiting the castle's staterooms during opening hours.

faqs.question: How much does it cost to visit Castle Fraser, and who manages it?
faqs.answer: Direct entry via the National Trust for Scotland, which has managed the property since it was gifted to the Trust in 1976, costs £18 for adults, £14 concession, £40.50 for a family ticket and £34.50 for a one-adult family. The castle, shop and tea room are open 10:30–16:30 with last entry at 15:30; the walled garden runs 10:00–16:00, and the wider grounds are open dawn to dusk year-round. Prices and hours are seasonal, so checking the NTS website before visiting is recommended.

faqs.question: What is a Z-plan tower house, and why is Castle Fraser considered a notable example?
faqs.answer: A Z-plan tower house is a Scottish fortification layout in which two towers project diagonally from opposite corners of a rectangular main block, giving defenders overlapping lines of fire along every wall. Castle Fraser, rebuilt on this plan in 1575 by Michael Fraser of Stoneywood and largely complete by 1636, is one of the largest tower houses in Scotland and widely considered one of the most elaborate and accomplished Z-plan examples in the country.
